topicName: Advanced SELECT Statements: DISTINCT, LIMIT, OFFSET
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Advanced SELECT Statements: DISTINCT, LIMIT, OFFSET"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"This tutorial explores advanced features of the SQL SELECT statement, specifically focusing on `DISTINCT`, `LIMIT`, and `OFFSET`. These clauses allow you to refine your queries, retrieve unique values, and implement pagination for large datasets."},{"order":3,"type":"heading","text":"DISTINCT Clause"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"The `DISTINCT` clause is used to retrieve only unique values from a column or a set of columns. It eliminates duplicate rows from the result set."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"Syntax"},{"order":6,"type":"code","text":"SELECT DISTINCT column1, column2, ...
FROM table_name
WHERE condition;"},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Example"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"Consider a table named `employees` with the following data:"},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"+----+----------+------------+
| id | name     | department |
+----+----------+------------+
| 1  | John Doe | Sales      |
| 2  | Jane Doe | Marketing  |
| 3  | John Doe | Sales      |
| 4  | Peter Pan| HR         |
| 5  | Jane Doe | Marketing  |
+----+----------+------------+"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"To retrieve a list of unique departments, you would use the following query:"},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"SELECT DISTINCT department
FROM employees;"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"This query would return:"},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"+------------+
| department |
+------------+
| Sales      |
| Marketing  |
| HR         |
+------------+"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can also use `DISTINCT` with multiple columns. In this case, the combination of values across the specified columns must be unique for a row to be included in the result set."},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"SELECT DISTINCT name, department
FROM employees;"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"This query would return:"},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"+----------+------------+
| name     | department |
+----------+------------+
| John Doe | Sales      |
| Jane Doe | Marketing  |
| Peter Pan| HR         |
+----------+------------+"},{"order":18,"type":"heading","text":"LIMIT Clause"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"The `LIMIT` clause restricts the number of rows returned by a `SELECT` statement. It's useful for retrieving a sample of data or implementing pagination."},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"Syntax"},{"order":21,"type":"code","text":"SELECT column1, column2, ...
FROM table_name
WHERE condition
LIMIT number_of_rows;"},{"order":22,"type":"subheading","text":"Example"},{"order":23,"type":"paragraph","text":"To retrieve the first 3 employees from the `employees` table, you would use the following query:"},{"order":24,"type":"code","text":"SELECT id, name, department
FROM employees
LIMIT 3;"},{"order":25,"type":"paragraph","text":"This query would return:"},{"order":26,"type":"code","text":"+----+----------+------------+
| id | name     | department |
+----+----------+------------+
| 1  | John Doe | Sales      |
| 2  | Jane Doe | Marketing  |
| 3  | John Doe | Sales      |
+----+----------+------------+"},{"order":27,"type":"heading","text":"OFFSET Clause"},{"order":28,"type":"paragraph","text":"The `OFFSET` clause specifies the number of rows to skip before starting to return rows. It's typically used in conjunction with `LIMIT` to implement pagination.  `OFFSET` is sometimes called `SKIP` in some SQL dialects."},{"order":29,"type":"subheading","text":"Syntax"},{"order":30,"type":"code","text":"SELECT column1, column2, ...
FROM table_name
WHERE condition
LIMIT number_of_rows
OFFSET number_of_rows_to_skip;"},{"order":31,"type":"subheading","text":"Example"},{"order":32,"type":"paragraph","text":"To retrieve the next 2 employees after skipping the first 1, you would use the following query:"},{"order":33,"type":"code","text":"SELECT id, name, department
FROM employees
LIMIT 2
OFFSET 1;"},{"order":34,"type":"paragraph","text":"This query would return:"},{"order":35,"type":"code","text":"+----+----------+------------+
| id | name     | department |
+----+----------+------------+
| 2  | Jane Doe | Marketing  |
| 3  | John Doe | Sales      |
+----+----------+------------+"},{"order":36,"type":"paragraph","text":"To implement pagination, you can adjust the `OFFSET` value based on the page number and the number of rows per page. For example, to retrieve page 3 with 5 rows per page, you would use `LIMIT 5 OFFSET 10`."},{"order":37,"type":"heading","text":"Combining DISTINCT, LIMIT, and OFFSET"},{"order":38,"type":"paragraph","text":"These clauses can be combined to create more complex queries. For example, you can retrieve a limited number of distinct values from a table."},{"order":39,"type":"subheading","text":"Example"},{"order":40,"type":"paragraph","text":"To retrieve the first 2 unique departments, you would use the following query:"},{"order":41,"type":"code","text":"SELECT DISTINCT department
FROM employees
LIMIT 2;"},{"order":42,"type":"paragraph","text":"This query would return:"},{"order":43,"type":"code","text":"+------------+
| department |
+------------+
| Sales      |
| Marketing  |
+------------+"},{"order":44,"type":"heading","text":"Important Considerations"},{"order":45,"type":"bullet_point","text":"The order of rows returned by `SELECT` without an `ORDER BY` clause is not guaranteed. Use `ORDER BY` to ensure consistent results when using `LIMIT` and `OFFSET`."},{"order":46,"type":"bullet_point","text":"The specific syntax for `LIMIT` and `OFFSET` may vary slightly depending on the database system (e.g., MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server).  Consult the documentation for your specific database."},{"order":47,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Using `LIMIT` and `OFFSET` without proper indexing can lead to performance issues, especially with large tables. Ensure appropriate indexes are in place."},{"order":48,"type":"heading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":49,"type":"paragraph","text":"The `DISTINCT`, `LIMIT`, and `OFFSET` clauses are powerful tools for refining your SQL queries. By understanding how to use them effectively, you can retrieve specific data, implement pagination, and optimize query performance."}]
